ops: The Rimborn speak Rimthal, the Threshold Speech, an oral language older than the Commonwealth and never written. Every statement in it describes a crossing, and speech names what is changing, in the order crossing, traveler, goal. Its roots are few and neutral: thur (crossing), azh (hearth), reth (road), varn (obligation), ven (pain), kai (hope). The spoken root carries the least of the meaning. Breath marks the kind of crossing, rhythm marks its state (begun, continuing, completed, broken), tone marks how the speaker knows it, and bearing (posture, gaze, hands) does the work of case. Silence is grammatical. Its non-verbal half, Vashrim, is shared with beasts, and Rimborn children learn both halves together. Commonwealth scholars have tried to transcribe Rimthal in Zeylaric, but that is a scholar's record of what he hears and not a writing system, and the Rimborn do not use it. ops: Scholária serves as the Commonwealth’s principal scholarly and academic language. Used by universities, learned societies, physicians, jurists, philosophers, and natural scholars, it provides a common medium for advanced study throughout the realm. It is not native to any people of the Commonwealth: it was codified in the Republic of Concordia and reached Zeythari through Concordian scholarship, law schools, and trade. While educated citizens may possess reading knowledge of Scholária, fluency remains largely restricted to academic and professional circles.

Scholária is closed to women: no woman is taught, speaks, or writes it, and a tutor who instructs a woman in it is subject to the penalties set out under Restricted Languages: Offenses and Penalties below.

ops: A deliberately evasive and adaptive criminal dialect spoken along frontier regions, ports, smuggling routes, and black-market networks. Its vocabulary shifts constantly, allowing speakers to communicate commerce that official authorities and Concordance inspectors were never intended to understand.

Women are prohibited from speaking it. A woman has no standing in criminal law, so the statute takes its measure in her body at the full extent instead: a woman heard using it is given the maximum correction, fifty strokes of the whip, administered publicly at the Bureau’s direction, and her master’s household is jailed and investigated for criminal association.

changes.new_text: Honorific Address: Every man must be addressed using formal markers of deference. The Lowered Tongue has three principal honorifics in Zeylara: Naevor (lord of a household — used for her master, husband, or guardian); Arglwydd (lord, a man of rank — used for nobles, officers, magistrates, and men of standing); and Syr (sir — the general honorific for any man whose rank she does not know or who holds no title). She addresses her master as Naevor, a man of rank as Arglwydd, and any other man as Syr or by his title. Omitting the honorific is a breach of the register, corrected as any other breach. The petitionary particles os gwelwch yn dda (if it please you) and gyda’ch caniâtâd (with your leave) precede any request. The phrase fel y mynnoch (as you will) opens any acceptance of a man’s direction.

Matter | Rule
Instrument | The Constitution is written and entrenched. It is the product of the Constitutional Settlement (see Section X), which in Realm Year 1780 (1380 A.K.) dissolved the old Kingdom of Zeythar and replaced it with the Commonwealth. Crown, Parliament, Assembly, Church, and Magistracy each hold their sphere under it, and no office stands above it.
Interpretation | The Magistracy alone. The full Grand Bench of fifteen sits on constitutional questions and may rule any law or decree unconstitutional.
Amendment | Passed by two-thirds of the Delegates of the Assembly and by two-thirds of Parliament, then given Royal Assent. An amendment touching oaths of office, the sacraments, or the order of the household also requires the concurrence of the Holy Synod. The marcher protections are entrenched and may be amended only by the same two-thirds vote in both chambers.

; serves four years; is discharged at twenty at the Confirmation Musters;
and is enrolled on the oath-roll kept by the
. Enrolment makes him a Zeythar, with the vote, the right to sue, and the right to speak before the Crown
. A man who fails his service surrenders his dagger and is never enrolled

Women | No woman is a citizen, a party, or an officer. She stands in law by her relation to her master or guardian, and every act touching her is his, brought and answered in his name.
Marcher protections | Each March returns a fixed bloc of Assembly seats that no redistricting may reduce, and the Office of Marcher Affairs hears frontier petitions as of right.

ops:
Division | Charge
The Register | Keeps the Commonwealth’s register of permitted garments and insignia by rank, profession, and oath-standing. Nothing is reserved, licensed, or forbidden unless it is entered here.
Heraldic Division | With the Office of Heraldry and Lineage, prevents unlawful appropriation of noble styles: reserved metals, gemstone arrangements, and the arrangements of the peerage in the caerwevra. A merchant’s wife may wear more gold than a baroness owns, but she may not wear it cut, set, or marked in a reserved pattern. That is impersonation, and the Magistracy treats it as such. It also screens the reserved arrangements in household braids and sandal straps.
Market Division | With municipal councils, regulates markets selling restricted goods and inspects stalls and goldsmiths for reserved cloth, metals, and stones.
Inspectors of Insignia | Inspect the markings of men and the forgeries of both sexes: the Oath Dagger and its Flame sigil and First Oath glyph, the hair-bound hilt, mandatory trousers, the parish pair-mark on a Band and its marriage dagger, and counterfeit Oath-Bands and caerwevrai. A man claiming protection, authority, or marital standing without the proper dagger markings is cited for fraud.
A man bearing an Oath Dagger without a Certificate of Citizenship (a Serviceman on his service book excepted) is arrested and referred to the Magistracy for the capital offense.
The Appraisers | Audit the dress of women throughout the Commonwealth. See below.

Heraldic Division | With the Office of Heraldry and Lineage, prevents unlawful appropriation of noble styles: reserved metals, gemstone arrangements, and the arrangements of the peerage in the caerwevra. A merchant’s wife may wear more gold than a baroness owns, but she may not wear it cut, set, or marked in a reserved pattern. That is impersonation, and the Magistracy treats it as such. It also screens the reserved arrangements in household braids and sandal straps.
Market Division | With municipal councils, regulates markets selling restricted goods and inspects stalls and goldsmiths for reserved cloth, metals, and stones.
Inspectors of Insignia | Inspect the markings of men and the forgeries of both sexes: the Oath Dagger and its Flame sigil and First Oath glyph, the hair-bound hilt, mandatory trousers, the parish pair-mark on a Band and its marriage dagger, and counterfeit Oath-Bands and caerwevrai. A man claiming protection, authority, or marital standing without the proper dagger markings is cited for fraud.
The Appraisers | Audit the dress of women throughout the Commonwealth. See below.

ops:
Matter | Rule
Strokes | Six at most for each woman in each audit, across the seat only, laid by the Appraiser or Inspector himself and never delegated to a Constable, a servant, or the master

. The exceptions are the Restricted Languages statute’s own measures: 24 strokes of the Cane for the Memory Layer, not fewer than 36 strokes of the whip for learning a prohibited language, fifty strokes of the whip for a woman heard speaking Skeinvash, and fifty strokes of the whip for a girl who persuades a tutor to teach her one. These are laid in public at the Bureau’s direction and are not audit corrections

.
Who may strike | The Appraiser and the Bureau of Weavefire’s Inspector are the only men in the Commonwealth, other than her own master, permitted to strike a woman, and within his own charge a male instructor. They alone may strike another man’s wife. Every other man (a Constable, a Warden, a parish steward, a Magistral, a Marshal, a soldier) who lays a hand upon a woman not his own commits an offense against her master.
Excess | A stroke beyond the sixth

, a stroke elsewhere than the seat, or a hurt beyond the passing mark of the Cane.
The master’s suit | A master (or guardian) who holds that the correction was excessive may sue the Office of the Appraisers before the Municipal Court of his district, with appeal to the Regional Court and the Grand Bench. The suit is his, brought in his name, and the woman is never a party. The finding of non-compliance is not before the Court. The measure of the correction is.
Remedy | The fine is paid first and recovered with the damages if the suit succeeds. The Court awards damages against the Bureau as it sets them, and the judgment is entered on the Appraiser’s Roll. Repeated entries, or one for injury, bring the Appraiser before the Registrar for removal.
The Bureau’s check | The Commissioner reads every Audit Roll, and an Appraiser whose findings depart from the norm of his district is audited in turn. An Appraiser who makes findings for gain or spite, or who takes any gift, is tried as any officer for oath-violation.
Outside his writ | Professed Sisters and every woman claimed by the Church (to touch a professed Sister is sacrilege, and the Church governs her dress entire; an Appraiser who sees one in fault reports it to her Confessor, who handles it); the Closed Naval Cities and the Servitor Quarters, which lie outside any civil circuit; and the Royal Household, which the Commissioner of Decorum for Kaervast reads at the Palace threshold (see The Royal Gown).
Constables | Crown Constables and Wardens assist an Appraiser when he asks (to summon a master, to collect a fine). They do not strike, and he has no power of arrest.

ops:
Matter | Rule
Nature | Not itself a religious body and not a foreign tribunal. Crown-owned and staffed by ordained clergy (the Magistrals), with a Harmonist of the Circle of Memory leased to each sitting to keep the record; consecrated jointly to Aequitus (Law) and Sophisra (Wisdom) as a matter of doctrine and oath, not divine jurisdiction.
Source of authority | The Constitution, the Oath of

, and lawful delegation by the Crown.
Divine mandate | None recognized in law. No judgment issues in the name of any god; no miracle determines guilt. Faith is permitted; divine authority is not.
Legitimacy | All lawful judgment derives from the Magistracy. No sentence binds unless rendered in its name.
Powers | Interpret law independently of Crown and Parliament; try all civil and criminal cases; rule laws unconstitutional; enforce property rights and contracts. Any person (a male citizen) may sue anyone, including the Crown. A woman is never a party; any suit touching her is her guardian’s, brought and answered in his name.
Magistrals | Citizens who have sworn the Oath of

and renounced foreign legal authority. They remain subject to Commonwealth criminal and civil law and are not exempt from prosecution, removal, or judgment by their peers.
Harmonists | Contractors, not members. Swear no civil oath and stand outside the Magistral’s chain entirely. Accountability runs through the Circle of Memory: the Amma of Harmony and the Archivist.

ops:
Position | Installation Method
The Crown | Hereditary agnatic primogeniture, House Karaya
Parliament (Peers) | Hereditary succession within the recognized Houses of the Maenari, the Satyrim, and the Maestrai (descended from unions between the other two), plus military-order courtesy seats
Assembly (Delegates) | Universal male suffrage among male citizens age 20+, service completed
Satrap | Elected by the male citizens of the satrapy (age 20+, service completed, Oath of

sworn), then formally confirmed by the Crown and required to swear a personal oath of accountability to it before taking office
Marshal | Crown-appointed from the senior officer corps of the Crown Regulars or the Order of the Standing Wall — a military command, not an elected office, given the frontier march’s standing war footing
Mayor | Elected directly by the male citizens of the town, under the same civic qualification as provincial elections
Chancellor of the Treasury | Nominated by the Assembly; confirmed by the Crown; personal oath of accountability sworn before he takes office
Magistral (Judge) | Aequiten Center formation (Concordia), twenty years’ combined clerical service, and secular law training, nominated by the Arbiter, appointed by the Crown, confirmed by Parliament
Crown Administrative Service | Meritocratic examination, followed by a sworn oath of service; hereditary appointment banned by law
Registrar of Civic Decorum | Crown Administrative Service: examination and oath; hereditary appointment banned
Appraiser of Civic Decorum | Examination in the sumptuary statutes and the Rule; two years’ probation under a senior Appraiser; oath sworn before the Office of Public Oaths
Chancellor (Keeper of the Seal), Spymaster, Royal Steward, Admiral of the Navy | Crown appointment; the Chancellor is confirmed by Parliament
Arbiter | Crown appointment; confirmed by Parliament
Speaker of the Assembly | Elected by the Delegates

ops:
Oath | Nature | Sworn by | Substance
The First Oath (Kyriel Aeloneth) | Sacramental; the oath itself is the sacrament | Every confirmed soul | One rite in every satrapy of the Communion; binds the swearer to Kairon for life. The boy swears the Oath of the Crowned (in Zeythari, the Vow of the Flame) before Kairon and Aequitus; the girl swears the Vow of the Faithful before Seraphiae and Sophisra
The Oath of

| Civil: confers no grace and creates no covenant with Heaven | Confirmed men only, immediately after the sacrament, before the parish Priest and the gathered garrison or township | To answer the Crown’s summons, stand where set, keep faith with the men beside him, and not abandon his post while breath remains: What I swear at sixteen, I shall owe at sixty. The Church witnesses and records it; the Crown holds the claim. Cowardice at the post is reckoned near kin to perjury.

The Oath of Citizenship | Civil: confers no grace and creates no covenant with Heaven | Men who have completed service, at discharge, at the Festival of First Oaths | To uphold the Constitution, defend the Realm, and honor the oaths that bind us. It completes the Oath of Muster. The Bureau of Citizenship enrols the man and issues his Certificate of Citizenship

The Vow of the Faithful | Sworn to Heaven in her own voice | Every confirmed woman | To remain faithful and chaste in body and word; to obey the man placed to rule over her, husband, father, or master, as Seraphiae obeys her Lord Kairon; to devote her life to righteousness and to the wisdom Sophisra grants; and, if she errs, to submit to correction and judgment. It binds unto death and is not released by the unworthiness of the man it is sworn toward.
The Vow of the Hearth | A public declaration, not a sacrament, not a binding oath, binds nothing at law. | Every confirmed woman, kneeling before Seraphiae’s image in the same hour as her Confirmation, witnessed by the parish Priest | Her obedience to her father until she is given in marriage, to her master from that day until death, and to any master set over her thereafter; faithfulness in the keeping of her household, modesty in bearing, dress, and speech, and steadfastness in the duties the Pattern assigns her. It puts her obedience on public records. A woman who later refuses her master’s lawful governance has gone back on her public word and broken her Vow of the Faithful
The Marriage Vow | Sealed in Seraval, the one word of a woman’s law of the realm acknowledges the instrument of transfer. | The bride | See Article VI

changes.old_text: Darlorath transfers once, from father to master at the Marriage Rite, and never again by act of man. A mastery held in trust for a term, under indenture or under a Crown or Church charter, is not a transfer of Darlorath. On the master’s death it descends to his heir and does not return to her father. The Forbidden Alienations are sale, trade or barter, pledge or surety against a debt, stake or forfeit at wager or at arms, lease, hire, or loan of the woman's person or mastery for any term. The contract of her labor or services by her master, wife or daughter, to the Crown, the Church, or a private party is not an alienation: Darlorath and the mastery stay with him, gift to another man as property, bequest as goods to anyone but the lawful heir, and surrender as blood-price. Two exceptions stand, and neither is a sale. The first is the indenture of an unmarried daughter by her father, approved by a Municipal Court under the Indenture Statute (Section VI). The second is the fixed-term service of an unmarried daughter, contracted by her lawful guardian to the Crown or the Church under charter. Each conveys a mastery in trust for the term and never the Darlorath (see Mastery in Trust, below). No plea of hospitality, necessity, or the woman’s assent serves in defense, since she has no assent to give. A plea of debt serves only as the ground of a petition under the Indenture Statute and never as a defense to sale. Whoever sells and whoever buys stands guilty of the heresy of the chattel: excommunication, delivery to the Magistracy, and execution under the civil code, the buyer hanged beside the seller. The recovered woman passes by ordinary descent, and no stain attaches to her.
changes.new_text: The Church holds that the Darlorath passes in the sacrament once, from father to husband at the Marriage Rite, and she knows no other sacramental transfer. The Church condemns as the heresy of the chattel the trading of a woman as goods: her sale, her barter, her pledge against a debt, her stake at wager or at arms, her gift as property, and her surrender as blood-price. No plea of hospitality, necessity, or the woman’s assent serves in defense before the Church. The offender is excommunicated and, since the Church does not bear the sword, is delivered to the Magistracy, which tries him under the Commonwealth’s law and not under this Article. The recovered woman bears no stain.

Boundary | Statement
1. Her life and her soundness | Her life is not his to take, and his discipline may not injure her permanently. A master who kills his wife forfeits the Darlorath, loses his standing among men, and stands before the Crown for a capital offense
2. Her sale | She is not chattel

2a. Her marking | No master may brand a woman. The brand is the mark of chattel, and she is not chattel. Magical glyphing and tattooing are lawful. A holder under a term of temporary Darlorath may mark her by neither, since her term ends with her returned “unmarked”
2b. Penalty for branding | Branding is a felony, tried by the Magistracy at the instance of her father or, failing him, the Crown. The sentence is five years’ hard labor and a fine to the Church of not less than 500 Zarims, since the Church keeps the household’s women during the sentence. The branded woman is healed at once by Aelorian physicians at the offender’s cost, and the healing does not wait on trial

3. The Three Closed Commands | He may not command her to murder, to renounce Truth, or to destroy an unborn child. A wife so commanded refuses, by silence and stillness and not by word or flight, and declares the command to her Priest. The burden of proving the command lies with her, and a false declaration is a graver offense than the disobedience she sought to avoid
4. The Seal of Confession | What she says to her Priest within the seal may not be used by any man against her. No master may demand what she confessed or punish her for having confessed
5. Her soul | The Final Reckoning holds her. She answers for her obedience, and her master answers for his governance of her

ops: Men and women are judged by different offices. The man is weighed on his oath kept or broken and on the governance of his household; the woman on obedience kept or broken, on devotion, and on bearing. Oath-breakers of either estate are counted among the gravest of sinners, and the woman who rebelled is counted an oath-breaker twice over, against her Vow of the Faithful and against the Pattern. Women reach the Reckoning through the intercession of Seraphiae, who pleads equally for every woman who has entered the Covenant, but whose intercession does not cover what a woman has not repented of. ops: Every confirmed man of every one of the nine peoples swears the Oath of

at Confirmation: four years’ mandatory active service to the Crown’s general levy, and a duty to hold his post beside any man beside him regardless of the people that bore either of them. Discharge at twenty ends active duty

seats him as a full citizen, but the oath itself does not lapse — the Creed states it directly, what a man swears at sixteen, he owes at sixty — and every discharged man remains liable to recall as a reservist for the whole of his confirmed life thereafter. This civil oath, laid atop the sacrament, is the actual mechanism that has held the peoples of the realm to one banner for nineteen centuries.

ops: Confirmed women swear no Oath of

, and the State takes no oath from a woman. A confirmed woman has four acts of sworn or declared word: the Vow of the Faithful at Confirmation, a binding oath sworn to Heaven; the Vow of the Rose, the Church’s vow made at her Veiling at twelve (the Litany of the Rose of the Holy Book of Truth and Grace); the Declaration of the Hearth, a public declaration of her obedience to her father and her intent to obey her master and any master after him, which binds nothing at law; and the Marriage Vow. The Church’s Order of Sisters keeps a parallel vow of steadfastness — not to abandon a granary, hospital, or garrison household under siege — a vow of the Church and not an oath of the State, regarded throughout the Commonwealth as equally binding, though its shape differs as the Pattern requires.

, and beneath it the Oath of the Oathguard, sworn to the Commonwealth. The Crown is served as its head.
Charge | The King, the Queen, the Queen Mother, the Heir and his wife, the Younger Prince, the three Princesses, the Assembly Hall, and the Hall of Memory and Stewardship.
Chambers | Men only. No girl of the Oathguard enters either Hall.
Livery | Its own. The Oathguard is the only Crown corps outside the standard livery.
Church | None. No Church order commands or disciplines an Oathguardsman.

Strength | 1,800 men: fourteen Hearths and a headquarters, about 257 Ninefold Files. One man of each people to a file; no file holds two of one people.
Captain | The Captain of the Oathguard, General grade, seated at Suraela. Appointed by the Crown.
Command | The Crown, openly, through the Captain. The Oathguard is not the King’s personal force.
Charter | Granted by Parliament. It may be dissolved only by the Assembly, then Parliament, then the Crown, in that order.
Pay | Voted by the Assembly in the military vote, as for the Army. The Crown does not pay it.
Oath | The Oath of the Standard, and beneath it the Oath of the Oathguard, sworn to the Commonwealth. The Crown is served as its head.
Charge | The King, the Queen, the Queen Mother, the Heir and his wife, the Younger Prince, the three Princesses, the Assembly Hall, and the Hall of Memory and Stewardship.
Chambers | Men only. No girl of the Oathguard enters either Hall.
Livery | Its own. The Oathguard is the only Crown corps outside the standard livery.
Church | None. No Church order commands or disciplines an Oathguardsman.

ops:
Matter | Rule
Eligibility | Unmarried women of eighteen and over, Presented. Commoner or noble households alike. A wife or widow cannot serve.
Term | Four years, non-renewable.
Payment | 100 zarims to the father on signing; a 300-zarim dowry paid to him on completion. Housed, fed, and clothed by the Guard.
Darlorath | Her father keeps the

for the term, through the Captain: her service, quarters, movement, dress, correction, and conduct, everything but carnal use. The Guard is not her husband. The father cannot recall her during service.
Sublease | The Guard may not lend, hire out, or assign her to any other man, house, or body. Doing so voids the lease at once and returns her to her father with her dowry paid in full, and the Magistracy censures the Captain.
Marriage | Courtship petitions go to her father, who may betroth her during the term. The wedding follows her release.
Intake | Three girls a year, in four classes of three.
Command | A man calls each girl’s work, always. A girl holds no rank and no authority over any man.
Discipline | The Guard’s own. The Head Girl corrects by instruction and chores and reports to the Captain. Corporal correction is the Captain’s or his delegate’s.
Grave breach | Dismissal to her father. The 300-zarim dowry is forfeit.
Speech and bearing | Articles IV, V, and IX at all times, in the Lowered Tongue.

arden, Keeper, Sentinel Captain, or their designated delegates. The Hearthguard hold no Rose

Eligibility | Unmarried women of eighteen and over, Presented and veiled. A wife or widow cannot serve
Contract | 24 months, renewable once (maximum four years), always signed by her father or legal guardian, who retains full coverture and may recall her at any time
Warrant of the Ward | Gives the Rose

. Must be signed by the father or lawful guardian who holds the Darlorath, or the contract is void.

Marriage | Marriage during the term ends the contract. Courtship petitions go to her father only, never to the Commander or the Rose

arden

Casting | Requires guardian’s written consent and Crown authorization. The guardian answers for everything she casts and delegates to the Commander the phrase of her glyph

ops:
Station | Rule Detail
Where | Inside a Crown citadel, its hospital‑works, or on the wall‑line; and, under a Maidenward Oath, at the forward aid post and in the field‑army camp. Never in a siege‑assault force or a sortie
Relief of the Archers | The 4,000 Citadel Arbalest maidens return some 4,000 Crown Archers to the field. In three watches, about 1,300 maidens stand on the wall at once, some 55 to a citadel
Drill | Practice bolts on the citadel range, within the walls, veiled, under the Rose

arden. No live fire outside the wall
Assault | A maiden fires only while her own citadel is under assault. She does not sally, advance, or pursue
Aerial Scouts | Sorties over Commonwealth‑held ground only, in an escorted pair with a Skyguard male, within the citadel’s signal range. Never over enemy‑held ground
Medical Extraction | Casualties are lifted from the wall‑side recovery line at the foot of the wall and, under Maidenward escort, from the field itself
Healing | Weave‑based, inside the walls or at a forward aid post, under a Sister of Light or an Army Surgeon
Reason | Aidion, Kaeyria, and the Ritebound Throne enslave captured women. A maiden under a Maidenward Oath is carried from the field before she can be taken. Her guardian signs against the Warrant of the Ward

arden or his delegate, performed often by the Sentinel.

arden, the surgeon, and the chaplain, each with the Matron. The Maidenward holds the wing gate from outside and enters only on cause (The Maidenward (the Sentinels))
Leave and visits | Leave is to her guardian’s house. Visitors are her father or his written delegate, in the Matron’s presence

ops:
Profile | Rule
Watch | Posted on the wall‑walk in three watches. She observes and reports to the Wall‑Captain. She does not fire
Alarm | The Wall‑Captain’s horn. She goes to her station by the stair she came up by, under her Oath
Assault | A maiden fires only while her own citadel is under assault, and only on the Volley‑Master’s call. She does not sally, advance, or pursue
Siege | Relief by the watch. A Volley Crew is relieved by its own crew, never in part. Quarrels are drawn from the post chest, and spent quarrels are counted back
Wall‑loss | The Order of Response governs (The Maidenward). The Sentinels carry her off the wall by the nearest stair
Practice | Blunt bolts on the citadel range, within the walls, veiled, under the Rose
arden. No live fire outside the wall

ops:
Matter | Rule
Status | Non-combatant. Bears no arms and swears no oath of the State. Indentured under the Indenture Statute (Section VI), in continuous guardianship.
Warrant of the Ward | The indenture instrument carries the Warrant of the Ward, and the Keeper’s Crown contract names it. The Warrant is the Keeper’s standing leave, given once, for the Sentinels of the Maidenward to address, restrain, lift, and carry her, and to strike her no more than twice on one occasion. It gives no leave for any labor or any carnal use. See The Maidenward (the Sentinels).
Contractor | The Keeper of the Maidens, one per posting. The Keeper is the master under the Statute.
Mastery in trust | The Keeper holds
, Mastery in Trust). Her father keeps the

. The Keeper is not her husband, and any carnal use is despoilment. He may not lend, hire out, or assign her to another posting, Order, or household. Doing so voids the instrument and returns her to her father with her dowry trust paid in full, and the Court censures the Keeper.
Pay | All pay goes to the Keeper. The Keeper pays the father’s debt into the Court and the Indenture Fee (125 Zarims) at registration.
Term | Four years, or until her twenty-second birthday if that comes sooner.
Collar and veil | As the Statute fixes. Collar always. Veil at Mass only, issued by the Keeper.
Liability | The Keeper answers for her conduct before the Magistracy, as a guardian answers.
Dress | Ordinary adult cut: mid-thigh, two-piece, undyed ash-linen, apron and cap. No Oath-Band, caerwevra, dagger, or rose badge.

, and his own officer answers for it. A Quartermaster who fails to investigate commits administrative misconduct. Her father, or any male citizen, may go to the Constable directly.

arden for a Thornmaiden or the Quartermaster for a Servitor

ops:
Rule | Effect
Offices are not ranks | The Warden of the Oath, the Admiral, and the Legate hold their grade by office. The Admiral’s rank exists only while he holds the Admiralty; on leaving it he reverts to his former grade and is addressed by it. The Warden and the Legate revert to General. The present Admiral is a Maenari peer; in uniform he is the Admiral and nothing else
Three peers | The Warden, the Admiral, and the Legate are equal in grade and precedence among themselves. None is the Commonwealth’s “Marshal”; none commands another. The Council of War is where their plans meet, and the Crown decides
Joint operations | For a named operation the Crown may by written order place a specific force (a Legion Chorus under the Admiral, a Marine Hearth under a Field Army, a squadron escorting an Army convoy, a Maidenward Half-Oath aboard a ship under the Admiral) under the operational control of the commander of the operation. The order names the force, the commander, and the term. When it lapses the force returns to its own chain
Operational and technical control | A commander of an army formation directs what an attached Weaveblade formation is to do. The senior Weaver present says how, and what it will cost. Discipline, training, and posting stay in the Legion’s chain
The Reckoning | Precedence is grade first, then commission date, never title or birth. A peer in uniform is addressed by his grade alone. Commissions are by examination and Crown or Marshal appointment; a Bandmaster or Deckkeeper may sit the examination
Joint precedence | Army, Navy, and Legion officers of equal grade rank by commission date
Women | Hold no rank and no command over any man. Thornmaiden offices (Rose

arden, Senior Maiden, Matron of the Rose) are unchanged and sit outside the ladder. Servitors hold no rank. A Matron’s, Stewardess’s, or Handmaiden’s word binds no Sentinel of the Maidenward.
Reserved title | Marshal of the Crown is reserved for the single command the King intends, in time, to place over every branch. It is not granted, and no officer holds it. Until it is, the three-peer arrangement stands
The Church orders | Keep their own structure and titles (see The Emberward Host: Command Structure below). Under the Warden of the Flame, as before

ops:
Matter | Rule
Order | The Order of the Veiled, House Zyrian, Roselight Circle. Its Sisters are the Veiled. No more than 200 at any time.
Who | Professed Sisters, celibate and perpetual, veiled, unringed, wearing no Oath-Band. Women of the Satyrim, Maenari, Maestrai, and Luminari. Mid Emberglow, Creation Thread. A Luminari woman qualifies only where her Prism reads Creation. Weave, not miracle.
Entry | By Church vocation (Roselight Circle), after the Hearthcoming.
Darlorath | Passes entirely to the Church on profession, as for every Sister. She holds authority over other women and none over any man.
Soul and title | Her Confessor keeps her soul and her title.
Mastery and discipline | While she is leased, the commander of the unit she is attached to holds operational and practical mastery of her and holds her discipline.

stays with the Church.
Lease | By commission, by name, and in writing, to the Crown, in the form of the lease of a Sister of Light.
Glyph | Struck on her Weavefire License. The Church, as her guardian, lodges the release. She is inspected by her Confessor or her Praesul alone.
Door | The Church’s lease, a fourth door into service beside the Contract Roll, the Warrant of the Pair, and the Handmaiden’s Hour. Open to the Veiled alone.
Vocation | Healing by Creation, embedded with the men she serves. Field miracle remains the Sisters of Light’s alone.
Arms | Unarmed work and the dagger. Nothing greater than a dagger.
Why she is the exception | The unit that holds her mastery is the unit that guards her. Licensed academies are forbidden to teach combat, and no other woman of the Church is taught it.
Dress | The Roselight habit in the convent. The Aurelian Veil System (Appendix O, M) in the field.

ops:
Provision | Rule
Legal personhood of women | Held in trust under Darlorath — vested in her father, then her master, then (if professed) the Church of the Sworn Flame; never self-held, at any age or rank. Church or Crown wardship of a wife or widow arises only under the Failed-Heir Clause
Property and land | Women hold no land, title, or office in Commonwealth law, of any of the nine peoples, without exception. A woman’s dowry, rendered at marriage or at religious profession, is the whole of any claim she will ever hold on her natal household’s estate
Inheritance | Passes through the male line without exception; this is Commonwealth civil law antecedent to Church doctrine, which ratifies rather than imposes it
Franchise | Assembly suffrage is restricted to male citizens who have completed their mandatory four years’ service (age 20+). Parliament seats and the Crown are hereditary in the male line exclusively
Marriage and consent | Petitioned by the man who holds her — father, brother, or guardian, or her local Praesul if she has none — and granted or refused by him alone. No court, testimony, or third-party approval attaches to the decision. At the altar each party’s assent is formally asked, as in the old rite; either may technically refuse, but the stigma falls on the refuser and his or her house for life, and refusal almost never occurs
Military obligation | Confirmed men swear the Oath of

at sixteen: four years’ mandatory active service, followed by reserve liability to the general levy until sixty. Confirmed women swear no oath of the State. The Church’s Sisters keep a parallel vow of steadfastness — not to abandon a hospital, granary, or garrison post under siege
Professed religious women | Profession is total, irrevocable transfer of Darlorath from household to Church. Reversal exists only through the Suit of Redemption — a Commonwealth national only, requiring the concurrence of the Praesul and the Canon Court, and rarely granted
Widowhood | Darlorath reverts to the eldest adult son or nearest male kin-guardian; a widow may be remarried at her guardian’s arrangement. The Church or Crown holds a widow only under the Failed-Heir Clause (see below)
Cross-racial application | Applied uniformly to Maenari, Satyrim, Duraken, Vykril, Avesari, Maestrai, and Luminari households alike under Commonwealth civil law, regardless of each people’s own inherited customs

ops:
Safeguard | Rule
Master’s interest | The master has paid a catastrophic debt and the fee for an asset he must return sound, unmarked, and marriageable. An injured, scarred, or despoiled girl costs him the asset, the price, and his standing. The law makes her care his interest.
Warrant of the Ward (Crown postings) | An instrument for a Crown posting carries the Warrant of the Ward: the master’s standing leave, given once, for the Sentinels of the Maidenward to address, restrain, lift, and carry her, and to strike her as needed. The Warrant creates no right to her labor and gives no leave for any carnal use. An instrument for a Crown posting without it is refused the seal.
Term | Four years, or age 22, whichever comes first, non-renewable by any master in any form. No woman is indentured twice. The Registry refuses a second entry.
No sale | Sale, trade, pledge, assignment, or transfer of the woman or of the instrument is the heresy of the chattel. Capital for seller and buyer (

). The instrument is void.
No despoilment | Any carnal use of her by the master, or by any man of his household with his leave or through his neglect, is a crime. Her willingness is no defense.
Return | She is returned to her father marriageable: intact, sound, and unmarked. On the date of release the clerk removes the collar and the Harmonist records the release. A Sister of the Solayan House may be asked to review her condition. Her review is information for the Magistral and certifies nothing.
Master’s record | A prudent master has a Sister of the Solayan House assess her at entry and at release, and has the assessment attested by the Quartermaster or another officer. It has no standing as certification. The Magistral weighs it with the rest of the evidence, as he weighs any record.
Redemption | The father or his kin may redeem her at any time by paying the master, through the Court, the debt the master paid, less a credit for the months she has served. The fee is not refunded. The Court orders the release, and the fee is entered in her dowry trust as on any release. The bar on a second indenture stands.
The collar | Plain ash-steel band, fixed by the Court’s clerk at registration. Struck with the Court seal, instrument number, master’s mark, and date of release. Removed only by the Court’s clerk on that date or on a Magistral’s order of release. The master may not remove it. A collar without a seal and a date is Kaeyria’s and Aidion’s, and is evidence of sale.
The veil | Suspended for the term. The collar replaces it as her mark of guardianship. Worn over the collar at Mass and sacramental occasions only. Restored at her father’s door on release.
Sumptuary law | Her unveiled face during the term is not an offense. No fine falls on father or master.
Her standing | The Registry records the term as service to her household. No stain attaches to her or to her prospects. No suitor may cite it against her in negotiation. The Registry’s entry of release is accepted by Priest and parish as proof of her standing.
His standing | The Registry and the parish record name the father’s failure. In her village the collar reads as his failure and her service.
Betrothal | Her father alone negotiates it, as for any daughter. The master holds no right in it whatever: he may not propose, grant, withhold, or take a price for it. Marriage follows release.
Master’s death, bankruptcy, or loss of his Crown contract | The Court releases her to her father. The instrument does not pass to a successor.

ops: Failure to complete service. A man who does not finish his term
surrenders his Oath Dagger to his parish Priest, never swears the Oath of Citizenship, is never issued a Certificate, and
remains a non-citizen. He cannot own property, marry, vote, or hold office; he pays special taxes; he bears social stigma
, and the missing dagger marks him
. Fewer than one man in a thousand fails.

ops: This marks complete male adulthood in Commonwealth law. What a man swears at sixteen, the Creed of the Sworn Flame states, he owes at sixty — the Oath of

does not lapse with his discharge at twenty. Completion of the fixed term retires him from active duty and seats him as a full citizen, but he remains liable to recall to the general levy as a reservist for the whole of his confirmed life thereafter, precisely as the Creed’s own reckoning implies. Most men marry between twenty and twenty-five, establishing a new household — the smallest and most vital unit of the Commonwealth.

ops: The Presentation is the largest ceremony of a girl’s formation, and the only one held at the community level. It falls at the same Confirmation Musters at which the young men of her year swear the Oath of

— the Church’s own Confirmation Rite, identical in sacramental form for both sexes, is common to both events; what follows the sacrament diverges sharply by sex, as Darlorath requires. For the young men it is the civil Oath of

. For the girl it is the Litany of the Veiled Rose, spoken over the year’s confirmed girls as the Holy Book of Truth and Grace provides, and, in the same hour, her Declaration of the Hearth: a public declaration, made before her father or guardian and the parish Priest, of her obedience to her father and her intent to obey her master and any master after him. It is not a binding oath, and no court receives it.

ops:
Ceremony | Age | Setting and attendance | Acts | Feast | Effect
Hearthcoming | 9/10 | Parish; the priest officiates; her household attends | The Devota (Handmaiden) who taught her places the hearthstone in her hands: polished volcanic stone marked with the First Oath glyph and Seraphiae’s flame. Her father formally receives her before the congregation | Modest; the family celebrates privately afterward | Completes Church schooling; formal return to her father’s guardianship. The hearthstone is personal, kept for life, and is proof of formation, blessing, and lawful return
Veiling | 12 | Parish church, before the altar of Seraphiae, on or near her twelfth birthday. Administered by the parish’s House Matron (its single Devota, ordinarily her primary Handmaiden); the parish priest attends | She speaks the Litany of the Rose (her Vow of the Rose) in white, without flowers or ornament; then her mother prepares the veil and places it over her face, speaking words that name what is being covered; her father formally declares his guardianship before those present. If the mother is dead or absent, the nearest female relative | None public; a private family meal; gifts modest and domestic | Knee-length dress and face veil of protected girlhood. Not marriage-eligible; approaches to her father are not appropriate

ops: The Foreign Education Exception is the Commonwealth’s one acknowledged inconsistency, and it knows it. Commonwealth law recognizes degrees earned at the following foreign institutions: Harborlight University at Reefhaven Commonwealth — the same institution Crown Prince Asyre himself attended, and, the University of Concordia at Scholar’s Rest in the Republic of Concordia, for religious, classical, and legal study.

ops: Every Confirmed man carries an Oath Dagger openly from Confirmation onward. It signifies acceptance of lawful violence when the Crown commands it, willingness to risk his life for Commonwealth and Crown, and submission to judgment should the Oath of

be broken. Unlike a sword or spear, the dagger is always present, always personal, and always intimate — the weapon of last resort, and for that reason the most honest one a man carries. A man who claims protection, authority, or marital standing without the proper dagger markings is guilty of fraud, and Commonwealth courts recognize the dagger itself as evidence of oath, proof of marital bond, and indicator of standing in any dispute where it is relevant.

ops:
Matter | Rule
Who | Every woman of sixteen and over: a sister, a wife, a widow. A girl of twelve to fifteen keeps her knee-length single piece. A professed Sister keeps the habit of her House entire and is outside this rule
Whose leave | The holder of her Darlorath: her father or guardian, her master, her eldest son or nearest male kin if she is a widow, and for a Thornmaiden the Rose

arden. A Servitor’s is the Keeper’s. Granted or refused by him alone. He may give it for a year, for a feast, or for a single service

When | At a church service: Mass, a sacramental occasion, a funeral, a wedding. She wears it to the service and from it by the shortest road. On a service morning on the church road, a long hem is presumed lawful and an Appraiser reads it as such. At any other hour or on any other road it is non-compliant and audited as such

Not exempt | The unescorted-woman rule. Article IX. The bar on male clothing. No long hem is cut as a man’s garment
Her option | She may attend in the standard hem. The permission is a leave and not an order. Many do in the High Heat
Expectant women | The Lysaran cord and the Longer Hem apply throughout the week. At a service she may wear either
Offense | A long hem outside the service rule is a non-compliant hem. Her master pays the Appraiser’s five Zarims, as for any non-compliant woman

Training Dagger | Age 12 | His father | Four inches, plain, serviceable. The dagger of preparation: you must now begin to think about what is coming
Oath Dagger | Age 16, on swearing the Oath of

| The parish, a licensed smith engaged by his household, or, where his father kept faith, his father’s own retired Oath Dagger | Personal and significant, but inherited, not earned: the blade of a son at the threshold of a man’s life
Marriage Dagger | The wedding | His bride’s household: her labor, her father’s connections, her brother’s effort. She places it in his belt with her own hands | A family sacrifice: a smith engaged through her father’s contacts, hours of domestic labor converted into value, a brother’s time freely given. Her labor belongs to her household, so the gift is the household’s. .

.

ops:
Nation | Relationship
Forest Realm of Zelesti | Formal alliance sealed by dynastic marriage — Princess Ilyara Thessandrion of Zelesti, a Maenari, to the Satyrim-blooded King Alexi Karaya, whose union produced the current, first-generation Maestrai sovereign. Zeythari holds a citadel-city on Zelesti’s frontier, ceded as part of the marriage settlement, guarding the forest road; Zelesti itself is a five-million-strong Maenari (high-elf) forest realm, magic-rich and steel-poor, whose rangers, archers, and mages are without peer on the continent but who cannot match a legion for numbers or a smith’s forge for steel. Its mage tower teaches pure magical theory in the manner of the classics, a counterpart to the Commonwealth’s Arcana Scholium; the Magitek Arcaneum, the Commonwealth’s research-and-development engine, has no equivalent in Zelesti.

The Maenari of Zelesti honor the Rimborn as Stewards of the Forests and find their keeping of their women abyssal, though the women are aligned to it and the Maenari are themselves a patriarchal and conservative people. Zelesti tolerates the Rimborn within its borders for two reasons: their effect on the Great Dark, and the alliance with Zeythari. No Great House of Zelesti or of the Commonwealth seeks a Rimborn clan for its daughters.

Kingdom of Kaeyria | An uneasy trade alliance rather than a friendship — functional, mutually profitable, and shadowed by the standing theological rupture between the Church of the Sworn Flame and Kaeyria’s own Church of the First Oath. Kaeyria is a feudal fortress realm holding the mountain passes north of the Great Zelesti Dark, connecting through to the Aidionic Empire on the far side; it borders Zeythari’s northwest borderland directly.

Forest Realm of Zelesti | Formal alliance sealed by dynastic marriage — Princess Ilyara Thessandrion of Zelesti, a Maenari, to the Satyrim-blooded King Alexi Karaya, whose union produced the current, first-generation Maestrai sovereign. Zeythari holds a citadel-city on Zelesti’s frontier, ceded as part of the marriage settlement, guarding the forest road; Zelesti itself is a five-million-strong Maenari (high-elf) forest realm, magic-rich and steel-poor, whose rangers, archers, and mages are without peer on the continent but who cannot match a legion for numbers or a smith’s forge for steel. Its mage tower teaches pure magical theory in the manner of the classics, a counterpart to the Commonwealth’s Arcana Scholium; the Magitek Arcaneum, the Commonwealth’s research-and-development engine, has no equivalent in Zelesti. The Maenari of Zelesti honor the Rimborn as Stewards of the Forests and find their keeping of their women abyssal, though the women are aligned to it and the Maenari are themselves a patriarchal and conservative people. Zelesti tolerates the Rimborn within its borders for two reasons: their effect on the Great Dark, and the alliance with Zeythari. No Great House of Zelesti or of the Commonwealth seeks a Rimborn clan for its daughters.
Kingdom of Kaeyria | An uneasy trade alliance rather than a friendship — functional, mutually profitable, and shadowed by the standing theological rupture between the Church of the Sworn Flame and Kaeyria’s own Church of the First Oath. Kaeyria is a feudal fortress realm holding the mountain passes north of the Great Zelesti Dark, connecting through to the Aidionic Empire on the far side; it borders Zeythari’s northwest borderland directly.

ops:
Matter | Fact
Designed and built by | Ironweave Works, the Duraken and Maenari engineering firm (“Ironweave”), under a standing Crown contract.
Age | About twelve years (first mounted ~1588 A.K.).
Deployed | Twenty, to date; the allocation is classified, and one of them stands in the Zelesti citadel.
Character | Huge, fixed engines mounted on citadels, crewed by small squads of mages clustered around them.
War record | None. They have never been fired in war. The Crown’s standing order is that they are not fired except in a declared war, so even the Shimmerwind skirmishes are fought without them.
Public knowledge | A foreigner who reaches a citadel wall may see a squad of mages gathered around a large mounted engine: unusual, but not evidently a weapon. The Magitek Arcaneum’s curriculum says only that “arcane weaponry” is taught.
Sites | Twenty engines in sixteen citadels; eight of the twenty-four citadels hold none. Ashward March: 6 engines in 5 citadels; Sundral: 5 in 4; Threnwood: 4 in 3; Zelesti: 1; the two Shimmerwind forts: 2; Hearthwall: 2 in 1.
Crew | About 26 Weaveblade to an engine: eighteen operators in three watches of six (Ritual Conclaves), four Spellwright Engineers, two Rune

inders, and two Silencers, plus four Ordnance Technicians of the Auxiliaries. Total strength is approximately 520 Weaveblade and 80 technicians, about 6.5% of the Legion.
The Ward-Yard | Each engine stands in a sealed, Crown-only precinct inside the citadel. Only career Weaveblade and Ordnance personnel enter; conscripts and Church brothers never do. The Ward-Yard answers to the commander of the Weaveblade Legion and the Warden of the Oath, not to the citadel Commander or the Castellan.
Cover | Officially a “resonance-ward battery.” Citadels already carry resonance-ward fortification and mage squads, so a cluster of mages at the wall draws no comment.
Testing | Ironweave test-fires every engine at its Duskhearth proving ground before mounting, using only its own staff; the Duraken insist on it. After mounting, crews drill dry on a low-draw crystal and never fire. The engines are land-mounted only; none is yet installed aboard a ship.
Who knows | Anyone who serves in a citadel knows there is a walled yard of mages and a large covered engine, much as they know the rail and the clean water. Almost no one knows what it does.

ops: Beyond the Ashward, Sundral, and Threnwood Marches lie two realms the Commonwealth has never annexed: the Margravate of and the Principality of . Each is feudal, each holds under a million subjects, and each keeps the Flame in the communion of the Sworn Flame. Parliament has declined to take either. Annexation would put their sixteen-year-olds under the Oath of

, their households under Darlorath law, and their walls on the Crown’s ledger, and it would buy the Commonwealth nothing it does not already have. A faithful neighbor that holds its own frontier is the cheapest line the realm owns. Parliament’s name for this is the Open March: the two realms are left their sovereignty, and the Commonwealth is left its choice of war.

ops: The line is held on purpose. A man who swears the Oath of

owes the women of the realm authority and protection, and so does the realm that rests on his oath. Neither realm has sworn anything, so the Commonwealth owes their lords nothing beyond what the Flame asks of any neighbor. But Parliament has never claimed that a Zeythari rescue waits on a foreign lord’s consent. When the Empire takes women, the Rangers cross the border, and whatever the margrave says of it afterward, he says to a realm that has already acted.

ops:
Realm Year | Astraian | Event
before the realm | c. 3,500–4,000 A.S. | The Subjugation: Aesylum falls to the Kyrillic Empire and the Satyrim are held five centuries as conquered property; the Zhaorya arise. (Dated in the old A.S. count.)
before the realm | c. 4,000 A.S. | The Rebellion: the Satyrim overthrow their occupiers and found the Kingdom of Jyotirai on the ruins of Aesylum
1 | 8,001 A.S. | King Vaethar Marren I founds the Kingdom of Zeythar and the city of Suraela; the First Standard tradition and the Ashward Palisade begin
c. 15–40 | c. 8,015–8,040 A.S. | The night at the Ashward palisade: the officer Thiras and a Satyrim garrison save the First Standard from the burning watchtower and swear the oath from which the realm’s oath-culture grows (retold in the later liturgy with five soldiers of five peoples)
63, 134, 198 | 8,063, 8,134, 8,198 A.S. | The First, Second, and Third Ashward Wars; the first stone wall-fort is built at Ashward
331 | 8,331 A.S. | The Compact of the Shimmerwind ends the first Shimmerwind Wars: the Kaelvash to the realm, the Wastes to the Vykril
c. 350–500 | c. 8,350–8,500 A.S. | The Avesari settle at Linhaven; the Maenari settle in the Threnwood as subjects
400 | 0 A.K. | The Visitation; the Astraian count passes from A.S. to A.K.
508–512 | 108–112 A.K. | The Vigil of the Standard; King Caelen VI converts, and in 512 decrees the Living Flame the official faith
560–619 | 160–219 A.K. | The Flame Wars, ended by the Council of the Five Standards (619)
738 | 338 A.K. | The Battle of Kaelvash: the Army of Light, the Great Compact sworn at Suraela, and the first Maestrai, born of the campaign’s camp marriages
780–850 | 380–450 A.K. | The Ashward Stone Wall is raised; Duskhearth is recognized as the Fifth Satrapy
892–920 | 492–520 A.K. | The Breaking of the Wall: the Ritebound grand invasion; Ashward sacked and the Walk of the Standard (893); the Grinding Years; the Citizen’s Oath language first codified (920)
c. 1000 | c. 600 A.K. | The Satyrim Exodus: a large body of Satyrim leaves Jyotirai for the Zeylaric valleys and joins the older Satyrim of House Marren’s frontier realm
1090–1178 | 690–778 A.K. | The Second Aidionic Wars, ended by the Treaty of Kharvesh (1178): the Shimmerwind caravan track is Zeythari territory
1163–1220 | 763–820 A.K. | The Council of Tongues forges Zeylara; it is mandated in the courts and the Warhost in 1220
1287 | 887 A.K. | The Treaty of the Threnwood with the Forest Realm of Zelesti; the joint Forest Road; the Zelesti citadel-city is pledged to the alliance
1421–1468 | 1021–1068 A.K. | Praesul Ordain Veldrath composes the Creed of the Sworn Flame
1603 | 1203 A.K. | The Holy See authorizes the Church of the Sworn Flame as a regional church of the Living Flame, about four hundred years before the present, after the Church in Zeythari had drifted from ordinary Living Flame practice into its own regional expression and an eleven-year examination (1592–1603); the Flameward is taken into the Church’s orders
1743–1752 | 1343–1352 A.K. | The Succession Crisis: King Caevorn XVII dies without a male heir; Parliament elects Lord Aldric Karaya (1752), a Maenari lord, over the male-line claimant; House Karaya begins its intermarriage with the surviving Marren lines, which continues for some four centuries
1768–1780 | 1368–1380 A.K. | The Great Parliament of the Seven; the siege of Suraela (winter 1779–80); the Constitutional Settlement and the Day of the New Oath (1780): the Commonwealth is proclaimed and citizenship opened to all nine peoples
Commemorated each year as Unification Day.

c. 1800 | c. 1400 A.K. | The Royal Bank of Zeythari is chartered at Solmara, two centuries before the present, during the expansion of the Guild Concordance; the Commonwealth’s state credit is thereafter routed through a bank neither Crown nor Guilds can command alone
1814 | 1414 A.K. | The High Council’s extraordinary session condemns Kaeyria’s Church of the First Oath as apostate, closing the corrupted reading of Darlorath that body had adopted
1932 | 1532 A.K. | King Alexi Karaya, a younger son elevated to heir after his elder brother’s death in a hunting accident, accedes
1947–1948 | 1547–1548 A.K. | The Marriage Settlement; Alexi marries Princess Ilyara Thessandrion, eldest daughter of the King of the Forest Realm of Zelesti; Zelesti cedes a frontier citadel-city as part of the marriage settlement
1952 | 1552 A.K. | Birth of Theron Karaya, the first Maestrai of the reigning line
1988 | 1588 A.K. | The first Arcano Cannon, designed and built by Ironweave Works under a standing Crown contract, is mounted on a citadel; twenty are deployed by the present, none yet fired in war
1996 | 1596 A.K. | King Theron Karaya ascends the throne on his father’s death, aged 44
1996–1998 | 1596–1598 A.K. | The Treaty of the Sands: the Shaelathi Tribe, largest of the Veyrathi tribes, petitions the Crown and is admitted by Treaty, ratified by Parliament and the Assembly, with two Assembly seats granted at admission, as the eighth people
1998 | 1598 A.K. | The Rimborn Asylum Accord: some two hundred thousand Rimborn refugees from the Ritebound Throne are admitted by King Theron’s Accord, ratified by Parliament and the Assembly, and settled in the Threnwood March as the ninth people. The first Rimborn citizens are enrolled at the Musters of 2000.
No Assembly seats are granted: Rimborn men vote for the Threnwood March’s delegates, most likely a Maenari.
2000 (present) | 1600 A.K. | Prince Asyre, Theron’s son and heir, marries a daughter of House Loravae, a landed Maenari peerage house

508–512 | 108–112 A.K. | The Vigil of the Standard; King Caelen VI converts, and in 512 decrees the Living Flame the official faith
560–619 | 160–219 A.K. | The Flame Wars, ended by the Council of the Five Standards (619)
738 | 338 A.K. | The Battle of Kaelvash: the Army of Light, the Great Compact sworn at Suraela, and the first Maestrai, born of the campaign’s camp marriages
780–850 | 380–450 A.K. | The Ashward Stone Wall is raised; Duskhearth is recognized as the Fifth Satrapy
892–920 | 492–520 A.K. | The Breaking of the Wall: the Ritebound grand invasion; Ashward sacked and the Walk of the Standard (893); the Grinding Years; the Citizen’s Oath language first codified (920)
c. 1000 | c. 600 A.K. | The Satyrim Exodus: a large body of Satyrim leaves Jyotirai for the Zeylaric valleys and joins the older Satyrim of House Marren’s frontier realm
1090–1178 | 690–778 A.K. | The Second Aidionic Wars, ended by the Treaty of Kharvesh (1178): the Shimmerwind caravan track is Zeythari territory
1163–1220 | 763–820 A.K. | The Council of Tongues forges Zeylara; it is mandated in the courts and the Warhost in 1220
1287 | 887 A.K. | The Treaty of the Threnwood with the Forest Realm of Zelesti; the joint Forest Road; the Zelesti citadel-city is pledged to the alliance
1421–1468 | 1021–1068 A.K. | Praesul Ordain Veldrath composes the Creed of the Sworn Flame
1603 | 1203 A.K. | The Holy See authorizes the Church of the Sworn Flame as a regional church of the Living Flame, about four hundred years before the present, after the Church in Zeythari had drifted from ordinary Living Flame practice into its own regional expression and an eleven-year examination (1592–1603); the Flameward is taken into the Church’s orders
1743–1752 | 1343–1352 A.K. | The Succession Crisis: King Caevorn XVII dies without a male heir; Parliament elects Lord Aldric Karaya (1752), a Maenari lord, over the male-line claimant; House Karaya begins its intermarriage with the surviving Marren lines, which continues for some four centuries
1768–1780 | 1368–1380 A.K. | The Great Parliament of the Seven; the siege of Suraela (winter 1779–80); the Constitutional Settlement and the Day of the New Oath (1780): the Commonwealth is proclaimed and citizenship opened to all nine peoples Commemorated each year as Unification Day.
c. 1800 | c. 1400 A.K. | The Royal Bank of Zeythari is chartered at Solmara, two centuries before the present, during the expansion of the Guild Concordance; the Commonwealth’s state credit is thereafter routed through a bank neither Crown nor Guilds can command alone
1814 | 1414 A.K. | The High Council’s extraordinary session condemns Kaeyria’s Church of the First Oath as apostate, closing the corrupted reading of Darlorath that body had adopted
1932 | 1532 A.K. | King Alexi Karaya, a younger son elevated to heir after his elder brother’s death in a hunting accident, accedes
1947–1948 | 1547–1548 A.K. | The Marriage Settlement; Alexi marries Princess Ilyara Thessandrion, eldest daughter of the King of the Forest Realm of Zelesti; Zelesti cedes a frontier citadel-city as part of the marriage settlement
1952 | 1552 A.K. | Birth of Theron Karaya, the first Maestrai of the reigning line
1988 | 1588 A.K. | The first Arcano Cannon, designed and built by Ironweave Works under a standing Crown contract, is mounted on a citadel; twenty are deployed by the present, none yet fired in war
1996 | 1596 A.K. | King Theron Karaya ascends the throne on his father’s death, aged 44
1996–1998 | 1596–1598 A.K. | The Treaty of the Sands: the Shaelathi Tribe, largest of the Veyrathi tribes, petitions the Crown and is admitted by Treaty, ratified by Parliament and the Assembly, with two Assembly seats granted at admission, as the eighth people
1998 | 1598 A.K. | The Rimborn Asylum Accord: some two hundred thousand Rimborn refugees from the Ritebound Throne are admitted by King Theron’s Accord, ratified by Parliament and the Assembly, and settled in the Threnwood March as the ninth people. The first Rimborn citizens are enrolled at the Musters of 2000. No Assembly seats are granted: Rimborn men vote for the Threnwood March’s delegates, most likely a Maenari.
2000 (present) | 1600 A.K. | Prince Asyre, Theron’s son and heir, marries a daughter of House Loravae, a landed Maenari peerage house

ops: The Veyrathi are a divinely crafted felid-hybrid people shaped by Obscyra, Goddess of Trickery, Secrets, Silence, and Lies, working alone from the magical residue of the Sundering. Long-dwelling in the Shimmerwind Wastes as neighbors to the Vykril clans, the Veyrathi — specifically the Shaelathi Tribe (People of the Tail / Expressive Line) — petitioned the Crown for membership in the Commonwealth and were formally admitted after accepting all terms of citizenship, swearing the Oath of the Standard, and converting to the Church of the Sworn Flame. They are the Commonwealth's second newest and second-smallest recognized people, and the only one whose entry was achieved entirely through diplomacy rather than compact, conquest, settlement, or asylum. Veyrathi live 185 to 220 years and breed true only among themselves; no pairing with another people has ever produced a child. They are distinguished by a striking sexual dimorphism: females present as nearly human in appearance, with human feet, fine velvet-soft patterned fur, a thin whip-like tail, voluntarily retractable claws, and extraordinary manual dexterity, while males are unmistakably felid, digitigrade, furred, long-clawed, and about twice a human male's strength. Both sexes share exceptional low-light vision, enhanced hearing and scent, and a patient, observational temperament; animal protein is the foundation of their diet, and their caloric needs run 20 to 25 percent above a human's. A Veyrathi woman is biologically bound in submission to her own master alone, her father, with her brothers as his deputies, until bonding, then her master; on widowhood, back to her brothers, and owes obedience to no man outside that chain. A rare gift, resonance, manifests exclusively in females, at Low Emberglow only; the few in whom it fully matures are the Luvia (officially: shaman), who see, heal, and call down lightning by instinct. The Veyrathi speak Veyr, a biologically imprinted language unique to their people and spoken by no other race in the Commonwealth.

ops: Its case structure is primarily derived from Saelkyr, the language of the former kingdom's Satyrim founders, whose five cases, vocabulary of covenant and law, and open flowing syllables the Council kept, and whose two registers, High and Low, it deliberately merged into one. Its core vocabulary, phonological foundations, and many everyday forms derive from Sailaeg. ops: Magic as engineering. The Commonwealth’s particular strength is that it treats magic as a science and integrates it with engineering. Pure theory has two seats: the Arcana Scholium at Suraela, and the Maenari mage tower of Zelesti, which teaches theory in the manner of the classics. They are two options for the same thing. The Magitek Arcaneum is something else, the Commonwealth’s research-and-development engine, which teaches magic as a trade at the forge and the loom of the Duraken guild-halls, with Maenari theory supplying the design. It is a quiet symbol of why the Commonwealth, and Ironweave Works in particular, can build things like the Arcano Cannon and the paired crystal: a realm that teaches theory alone does not produce them, and a realm that teaches a trade alone does not design them.

ops: The Veyrathi of the Commonwealth are exclusively the Shaelathi Tribe, numbering approximately 400,000 souls. The Shaelathi are not merely the largest Veyrathi tribe, but the first and only true Veyrathi mega-tribe. While most tribes number fewer than 50,000 members, the Shaelathi were formed through the gradual union of numerous smaller tribes under a single authority, ultimately growing to encompass nearly one-fifth of the entire Veyrathi population. ops: No individual was more important to that process than Marshal Grakhal Vrakhur-zan. ops: Veyrathi live between 185 and 220 years and breed true only among themselves; no pairing between a Veyrathi and another people has ever produced offspring. Males are unmistakably felid, with digitigrade legs, dense fur, long claws, and physical strength approximately twice that of a human male.

ops: The Rimborn are an unthreaded people, the children of Tessara, the Greenwarden, and Caedron, Lord of Stewardship, born in the age after the Betrayal of the Veritarch to two gods for whom the Weave had made no provision. ops: Long scattered along the forest margins of the continent, the Rimborn were driven from the Ritebound Throne's woodland territories between R.Y. 1994 and 1998. Nearly two hundred thousand crossed the Ashward March seeking refuge within the Commonwealth. The Crown admitted them under the Rimborn Asylum Accord, granting asylum and settlement rights in what became the Threnwood March. Unlike every other recognized people of the Commonwealth, the Rimborn entered the realm not by treaty, conquest, or incorporation, but as refugees.

ops: For a generation they remained under asylum protection. In time, Rimborn leaders petitioned the Magistracy for citizenship. ops: For this reason, the Rimborn occupy an anomalous position within Commonwealth law and society. Protected by the Crown and entitled to citizenship, they nevertheless remain a people originally admitted under asylum who simply never departed. Their settlements in the Threnwood March are therefore administered under a special regime. Rather than falling under the ordinary jurisdiction of a satrap, they are overseen by the Warden of Threnwood, a Crown officer exercising both military and civil authority. The Warden serves simultaneously as protector, governor, and observer, a living expression of the Crown's determination that the Rimborn remain secure, orderly, and closely watched.

ops: Zeylara is a deliberate synthesis of six source traditions, each contributing distinct and irreplaceable elements. Its grammatical skeleton — masculine-default gender, lineage suffixes, and formal syntactic structure — derives primarily from Lórenei, the tongue of the Maenari, which the Council adopted and simplified. Its phonological foundations, core vocabulary, consonant mutation system, and poetic tradition derive from Sailaeg, the Council’s constructed Base, which provided the language’s Celtic sound and flow. Its case ending (the accusative suffix -an) and its long-vowel emphasis system derive from Durakhtûn, the tongue of the Duraken guilds. Its volitional verb system — the celebrated cae- (chosen present), zae- (chosen past), and thae- (sworn future) — and its emotional and collective vocabulary derive from Avesai, the tongue of the Avesari, whose philosophy that choice is the highest moral act is encoded into Zeylara’s grammar itself. Its evidential system — the four markers of how a speaker knows what is claimed (-ka witnessed, -thu reported, -mor tradition, -var ancestral) — its oath vocabulary, and its martial consonant clusters derive from Khor’dal, the tongue of the Vykril clans. From Saelkyr, the tongue of the Satyrim, the Council drew the language’s philosophical and sacred vocabulary: santh (covenant, binding accord), vereth (sacred truth, distinct from the everyday vorai), concordia (harmony), serin (chosen submission), auria (holy light), eloria (wisdom), and eternum (eternity). Saelkyr also contributed the Sacred/Luminal noun class — the grammatical category that allows the Dyarchy theology to function without subordinating either divine being to the other — the VSO word-order inversion of the Memory Layer, and the sa- relational construction used in ancestral address and funeral elegy. What the Council deliberately rejected from Saelkyr was not its vocabulary or its philosophical architecture, but its socially enforced two-register system (Saelkyr Vael for the high-born, Saelkyr Domen for the low), in accordance with the mandate of no class in the grammar. The Five Mandates were honored in full: every founding tongue contributed to Zeylara, no people were permitted to claim it as merely their language under another name, and the result was a language in which every citizen of the Commonwealth can hear the echo of their own ancestral tongue.

ops: The Vensharic tongues are closed to women. No woman is taught, speaks, or writes Venshal, Tesshare, or Skeinvash; she speaks for her master’s shop or stall in Zeylara, in the Lowered Tongue, as his deputy.

ops: Scope of the bar. Common is a full register of Zeylara: complete for household, market, parish, and school, and missing only the civic, legal, military, and governing registers. Zeylara is the only official language of the Commonwealth, and a woman is not a civic actor: she is escorted in public at all times and has no business that needs a civic voice. The bar therefore covers every register of Zeylara above Common and Hearth, and every language of the sacred, learned, and commercial layers (Seraval, Scholária, Venshal, Tesshare, Skeinvash). It binds every woman without exception, professed Sisters included. The Commonwealth does not regulate the ancestral tongues and does not teach them formally. A woman may be fluent in Lórenei, Saelkyr, Avesai, Durakhtûn, Khor’dal, Veyr, or Rimthal and still be restricted to Common and Hearth in Zeylara. Where a woman writes, she writes in Common Zeylaric (the Common Hand, Llaw Gyffredin) at her master’s behest and never as an autonomous agent; devotional texts are written in Common, and every other writing is done by her master’s leave. A woman may copy and illuminate a text in a restricted language as a hand, without reading it. A woman who translates renders Common and Hearth Zeylara into an ancestral tongue, never the reverse.

ops:
Offense | Who answers | Penalty
A woman speaks or writes a restricted register or language: Formal, Legal, Military, Seraval, Scholária, Venshal, or Tesshare (the Memory Layer and Skeinvash are measured apart; see below) | The woman; her master | Six strokes of the Cane; master fined 10 Zarims. Per offense. Private discipline at the master’s discretion.
A woman speaks, recites, or writes the Memory Layer: in verse, at a funeral, in ceremony, or in an Appraiser’s hearing | The woman; her master | 24 strokes of the Cane at the town post, laid publicly at the Bureau’s direction; master fined five to twenty Zarims, per offense. Measured at four times an ordinary lapse of the tongue, and the censure is entered against the household. Private discipline at the master’s discretion thereafter.
A woman is found to have learned a prohibited language, whether she was taught it or coaxed it | The woman; the tutor | Not fewer than 36 strokes of the whip at the town post, laid publicly at the Bureau’s direction; she is then returned to her master for such private discipline as he judges fit. The whip and not the Cane: the offence is a breach of the sumptuary statutes, not a lapse of household manners. Where she coaxed or encouraged her tutor, 50 strokes, as in the last row below.
A woman is heard speaking Skeinvash (Under-Cant) | The woman; her master | Fifty strokes of the whip at the town post, the maximum, laid publicly at the Bureau’s direction, and her master’s household is jailed and investigated for criminal association. Per offense.
A woman writes anything other than devotional texts in Common without her master’s leave, or writes in her own name | The woman; her master | The same: six strokes of the Cane; master fined 10 Zarims. Per offense.
A master hires a tutor specifically to teach a woman of his household a restricted language | The master | Fined 10 Sol. A tutor who refuses the commission is not fined.
A tutor teaches a woman a restricted language | The tutor | Fined 10 Sol; his teaching licence is at risk, and on a second offence it is revoked permanently. If he was hired for a permitted subject and added the language on his own, the master is not fined. If the master hired him for the language, the master is also fined under the row above.
A girl persuades a tutor hired for a permitted subject to teach her a restricted language | The girl; the tutor | Girl: 50 strokes of the whip at the town post, laid publicly by the Appraiser. Tutor: 10 Sol, and his licence and professional standing at risk.

ops: Enforcement. The Bureau of Civic Decorum assesses every fine above on the Appraiser’s finding alone. A master who disputes a finding may sue the Office of the Appraisers under Limits and the Master’s Remedy. Ten Sol is about two hundred Zarims, and the fine is set high enough to make the instruction of women in restricted languages ruinous to any tutor who attempts it. A tutor has no authority to strike or discipline a woman. In this statute the Appraiser administers the punishment himself, in public, and needs no leave from her master. The six strokes are the price of a failed audit and not a punishment: they are laid where she is found and finished at once, for any sumptuary infraction in her dress, her bearing, or her speech, and the audit closes with them. The heavier measures are not a failed audit. They are punishments: ordered by the Bureau, laid at the town post, in public, and entered against the household as a censure. Private discipline for any of these offenses remains at her master’s discretion under Article IX, and a master needs no permission to punish what is his.

ops: Bureau of Citizenship — A sub-office of the Royal Census and Demography Office. Keeps the oath-roll, issues the Certificate of Citizenship to each man who swears the Oath of Citizenship at discharge, and answers every Inspector’s, magistrate’s, and clerk’s inquiry as to whether a man stands on the roll. Receives the Warhost’s muster rolls and the Office of Public Oaths’ record of the Oath of Muster, records every surrender of an Oath Dagger, issues the Writ of Replacement for a lost dagger, strikes the roll on a Magistral’s conviction, and lodges its fair copy with the Circle of Memory.

The Town Post

ops: The town post stands in the public square of every Commonwealth town that keeps a market, and at the gate of every satrapy seat, and it is the Crown’s and not the parish’s. In the lesser towns it is a squared oak upright taller than a man; in Suraela and at the satrapy seats it is ash-steel set in a stone plinth. A cross-bar runs at the height of the hip with a staple at either end, and above it, at the height of the hands, an iron ring is set in the post. It is not a gallows, and no execution is done at it.

ops: For the Cane the woman is bent over the cross-bar, feet apart and set back, her wrists closed in the staples at either end, so that the seat is held to the line of the stroke and she can neither rise nor turn. For the whip she is stood to the post and her wrists are taken up to the ring above her head, which draws her out and opens the back, and the whip may fall on the back as well as the seat, which the Cane may not. In either position she is held by the iron and by no man’s hand: no Appraiser, Constable, or servant grips her, and this is what the staples are for.

ops: The strokes are laid by the Appraiser himself, or by one of the Bureau of Weavefire’s Inspectors where the matter is his, and never by another man. A Constable keeps the square and summons the master; he does not strike, and he does not hold her. The warrant is read before the first stroke and the correction entered on the Roll after the last. A master who owes the Crown a public correction may bring it to the post, but the post is the Crown’s, and the Appraiser has the first claim on it.

ops: This Article is canon law. It states what the Church teaches and what the Church enforces within her own jurisdiction: her sacraments, her censures, her clergy, and the consciences of the Faithful. It is not the civil law of the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth keeps its own law of the Darlorath, made by the Crown and Parliament and adjudicated by the Magistracy (see Commonwealth Law of the Darlorath, below), and it holds every right to pass, amend, and adjudicate that law without the Church’s leave. The Church speaks to the soul and the Commonwealth to the state, and neither Article nor statute amends the other. This Article is changed by the Holy Synod alone.
